title: Stroke Is an Emergency: How to Recognise It, Act Fast, and Support Recovery
excerpt: Stroke can happen suddenly, but knowing the warning signs and acting immediately can change the outcome. Learn how to use BEFAST, what to do while help is coming, and how families can support recovery after hospital treatment.
content:
## Why Every Minute Matters
A stroke occurs when part of the brain is deprived of blood flow or when a blood vessel in the brain bleeds. Brain cells are highly sensitive to this interruption, so treatment should never be delayed while waiting for symptoms to improve. Fast recognition and early treatment can reduce brain injury and disability.

Stroke is not only a concern for older adults. The risk may increase with uncontrolled blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, heart rhythm problems, obesity, and a previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Regular health checks and consistent treatment of these conditions are important parts of prevention.

## Learn BEFAST
The BEFAST test is a simple way to remember several common warning signs. It is not a substitute for medical assessment; if even one sign appears suddenly, treat it as an emergency.

| Letter | Warning Sign | What to Look For & Simple Check |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **B — Balance** | Sudden dizziness, unsteadiness, or difficulty walking | Ask whether the person suddenly feels off-balance or cannot walk steadily. |
| **E — Eyes** | Sudden loss or change of vision | Ask whether vision has become blurred, doubled, or missing in one or both eyes. |
| **F — Face** | Drooping or numbness on one side | Ask the person to smile and look for an uneven or lopsided smile. |
| **A — Arms** | Weakness or numbness, particularly on one side | Ask the person to raise both arms and check whether one arm drifts downward. |
| **S — Speech** | Slurred, confused, unusual, or absent speech | Ask the person to repeat a simple sentence and check for slurring. |
| **T — Time** | Time to seek emergency help | Note when symptoms began (or last known well time) and call 112 immediately. |

Sudden severe headache without a known cause, new confusion, or weakness in a leg can also be a warning sign. Symptoms that disappear after a few minutes may represent a TIA. A TIA is still a serious medical warning and should be assessed urgently rather than ignored.

## What to Do When Stroke Is Suspected
- **Call 112 immediately:** Call India’s integrated emergency number (112) and clearly state that you suspect an acute stroke.
- **Note the exact time:** Record the exact time symptoms were first noticed, or the last time the person was completely well. This crucial information influences acute neurovascular treatment decisions like thrombolysis (clot-busting medication).
- **Keep the person safe and comfortable:** Keep them rested in a comfortable position while help is on the way.
- **Do NOT give food, water, or oral tablets:** Swallowing may be impaired, posing a severe choking hazard.
- **Do NOT ask the person to walk:** Sudden weakness can cause dangerous falls. Avoid driving them yourself if an emergency ambulance is available.
- **Prepare medical records:** Keep a list of current medicines, allergies, and major medical conditions ready for the emergency team.
- **Do NOT wait to see if symptoms improve:** Some treatments are strictly time-dependent, and the safest course is rapid assessment at a hospital equipped to manage acute stroke.

## Recovery Begins After the Emergency
Leaving the hospital is not the end of stroke care. Recovery may involve a neurologist, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech and swallowing therapist, psychologist, dietitian, and trained caregivers.

The World Health Organization’s rehabilitation framework recognises the need for structured interventions, assistive products, equipment, and a skilled rehabilitation workforce for neurological conditions, including stroke.

The rehabilitation plan should be individualised. One person may need help with walking and balance; another may need speech therapy, swallowing assessment, memory support, or treatment for mood changes. Families can help by attending follow-up visits, maintaining a medication routine, reducing fall hazards, encouraging prescribed exercises, and reporting new or worsening symptoms promptly.

## Preventing Another Stroke
Prevention is a continuing process. Take prescribed medicines consistently, monitor blood pressure and blood sugar as advised, stop smoking, remain physically active within your clinician’s recommendations, choose a balanced diet, and attend follow-up appointments. Never stop an antiplatelet, anticoagulant, blood-pressure medicine, or other treatment without medical advice.

A stroke can be frightening, but timely action and organised follow-up can make a meaningful difference. Remember: **BEFAST, call 112, and do not delay.**

## When to Seek Urgent Help
Call 112 immediately for sudden facial drooping, one-sided weakness or numbness, new speech difficulty, sudden visual loss, severe imbalance, or an unexplained severe headache. If symptoms have already resolved, seek urgent medical evaluation because a TIA may precede a major stroke.

### References
1. CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Stroke
2. Government of India: Emergency Response Support System 112
3. WHO: Package of Interventions for Rehabilitation — Module 3: Neurological Conditions

title: Patient Care in Neurological Disorders: A Practical Guide for Patients and Families
excerpt: Neurological disorders often affect movement, memory, speech, mood, sleep, and independence. A practical care plan—built with the patient, family, and healthcare team—can improve safety, confidence, and day-to-day quality of life.
content:
## Neurological Care Is More Than a Prescription
Neurological disorders include conditions affecting the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles. Examples include stroke, epilepsy, Parkinson’s disease, migraine, dementia, neuropathy, multiple sclerosis, and disorders of movement or balance. Each condition is different, and even two people with the same diagnosis may have very different symptoms and goals.

Good care therefore begins with an accurate diagnosis and a shared plan. The plan should address symptoms, treatment, safety, function, emotional wellbeing, and the patient’s priorities—not only the scan or test result.

## Build a Care Plan Around Six Questions

| Care Area | Questions to Discuss with the Neurologist |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1. Diagnosis** | What is the working diagnosis, and which tests or follow-up visits are needed? |
| **2. Treatment** | What is each medicine or therapy for, and when should it be taken? |
| **3. Function** | Is there difficulty with walking, balance, speech, swallowing, memory, work, or daily activities? |
| **4. Safety** | What situations create risk at home, at work, while bathing, or while travelling? |
| **5. Monitoring** | Which symptoms should be recorded, and which changes require urgent help? |
| **6. Goals** | What matters most to the patient over the next few weeks and months? |

Writing these answers down can prevent confusion, especially when several family members are involved. Bring a current medicine list, previous reports, imaging discs or links when available, and a short record of symptom changes to appointments.

## Medication Safety and Follow-Up
Many neurological treatments work best when taken consistently. Use a pill organiser, phone reminder, or family-supported schedule if helpful. Never double a missed dose or stop a medicine suddenly without asking the prescribing clinician; the correct action depends on the treatment and the condition.

Families should watch for new side effects, excessive sleepiness, falls, confusion, allergic reactions, or a change in seizure frequency. A symptom diary can be particularly useful for headaches, tremor, medication response, sleep, and seizures. It should record the date, time, duration, triggers if known, and recovery—not just a general statement that the symptom was “worse.”

## Rehabilitation and Preserving Independence
Rehabilitation is not limited to the first days after a stroke. Depending on the diagnosis, it may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, swallowing support, cognitive rehabilitation, psychological care, or assistive devices.

The World Health Organization’s neurological rehabilitation package includes stroke, Parkinson disease, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, and dementia, and emphasises essential interventions and the workforce and equipment needed to deliver them.

The goal is meaningful function. That may mean walking more safely, using the hand for dressing, communicating clearly, returning to a valued activity, or managing fatigue. Short, regular practice that follows the prescribed programme is generally more sustainable than pushing through severe exhaustion or pain.

Patients and caregivers should also ask whether the home needs changes. Better lighting, non-slip bathroom surfaces, handrails, clear walking paths, suitable footwear, and supervision during higher-risk activities may reduce preventable injuries. Any exercise or equipment plan should be tailored to the person’s diagnosis and physical ability.

## Nutrition, Sleep, Mood, and Communication
Regular meals, hydration, appropriate physical activity, and a consistent sleep routine support overall health, but there is no single “neurological diet” that replaces diagnosis-specific treatment. Ask the clinician or dietitian about swallowing difficulty, diabetes, kidney disease, medication-food interactions, or unintended weight loss.

Depression, anxiety, irritability, apathy, and caregiver exhaustion are common but often overlooked. They are not a sign of weakness and should be discussed openly. A patient who is struggling emotionally may need counselling, medication review, social support, or a change in the rehabilitation plan.

Communication should preserve dignity. Speak directly to the patient, allow extra time for answers, reduce background noise, and avoid completing every sentence unless the person asks for help. Encourage independence where it is safe, while providing support for tasks that truly require assistance.

## When Symptoms Need Urgent Attention
Seek emergency help for sudden face or limb weakness, new speech or vision difficulty, severe breathing problems, a prolonged or repeated seizure, a major injury, sudden loss of consciousness, or a severe new headache with neurological symptoms. In India, call 112 for an emergency and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A routine appointment is appropriate for gradual changes, recurring headaches, increasing tremor, medication concerns, or new sensory symptoms, but waiting for a scheduled visit is not appropriate when symptoms are sudden or severe.

## The Best Care Plan Is Shared Care
Patients do not have to manage a neurological disorder alone. The neurologist provides diagnostic and treatment direction; therapists support function; nurses and caregivers help with daily routines; and families contribute observations, encouragement, and practical safety measures. Most importantly, the patient remains an active partner in decisions.

With clear information, realistic goals, regular follow-up, and timely escalation of warning signs, neurological care can become more organised and less overwhelming. Small, consistent steps often build the foundation for greater safety and independence.

For a personalised neurological evaluation and care plan, schedule a consultation with Dr. Pratik Kishore at Neuropoint Medical Centre, New Delhi.

2. Government of India: Emergency Response Support System 112

title: BEFAST for Stroke—and What to Do When a Seizure Looks Similar
excerpt: BEFAST is a stroke-recognition tool, not a seizure first-aid mnemonic. Learn how to use BEFAST correctly, how seizures may mimic stroke, and the safest steps to take when someone is having a seizure.
content:
## An Important Clarification About BEFAST
BEFAST stands for Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, and Time. It helps bystanders recognise possible stroke symptoms and seek emergency care quickly. It should not be rewritten as a seizure checklist. A seizure may cause unusual movements, staring, impaired awareness, confusion, or temporary weakness, and some of these symptoms can overlap with stroke. Because the cause cannot always be determined safely at home, a new or unexplained neurological event needs prompt medical assessment.

The practical update is simple: **use BEFAST for suspected stroke, and use seizure first aid when a seizure is occurring.** When there is uncertainty—especially with a first event—call for emergency help.

## Use BEFAST When Symptoms Are Sudden

| Letter | Stroke Warning Sign | What to Do & Look For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **B — Balance** | Sudden dizziness, unsteadiness, or loss of coordination | Keep the person from walking and note when symptoms began. |
| **E — Eyes** | Sudden change or loss of vision | Ask what they can see, without delaying the emergency call. |
| **F — Face** | One-sided facial drooping or numbness | Ask them to smile if they can do so safely and check symmetry. |
| **A — Arms** | One-sided weakness or numbness; one arm may drift down | Ask them to raise both arms only if safe. |
| **S — Speech** | Slurred, strange, confused, or absent speech | Ask for a simple sentence and check comprehension. |
| **T — Time** | Time to activate emergency care | Call 112 in India and record the last-known-well time. |

Sudden severe headache, new confusion, or weakness in a leg may also indicate stroke. Even if the symptoms improve, urgent assessment remains important because a TIA can be a warning of a future stroke.

## What a Seizure May Look Like
A seizure does not always involve dramatic shaking. Some people stare blankly, become unresponsive, repeat an automatic movement, suddenly stiffen, or appear confused. Others may fall and have rhythmic jerking. Most seizures last only a few minutes, but timing the event is essential.

After a seizure, the person may be sleepy, confused, or have temporary weakness (known as Todd's paresis). Temporary weakness on one side after a seizure can resemble stroke. It is not safe for a bystander to assume that weakness is “only post-seizure,” particularly if the event is new, the recovery is atypical, or other BEFAST signs are present.

## Seizure First Aid: Protect, Observe, and Time
- **Stay calm and remain with the person:** Note the time the seizure began and monitor throughout.
- **Make the space safe:** Move nearby hard or sharp objects away, cushion the head with something soft and flat, loosen tight clothing around the neck, and remove glasses if possible.
- **Place in recovery position:** If the person is on the ground, gently turn them onto their side when practical, with the mouth angled toward the ground, to help keep the airway clear.
- **DO NOT restrain the person’s movements:** Let the seizure run its course without physical restraint.
- **DO NOT put anything in the mouth:** Do not put a spoon, fingers, medicine, water, or any other object in the mouth. Do not offer food or drink until the person is fully alert.
- **DO NOT attempt mouth-to-mouth breathing:** Breathing will normalize naturally once the seizure stops.
- **After movements stop:** Speak gently, explain what happened, and help the person recover in a safe place. If they have a medical identification bracelet or an individual seizure plan, check it when safe to do so.

## When to Call Emergency Services (112)
Call 112 immediately if:
- The seizure lasts **longer than five minutes**.
- Another seizure starts before the person fully recovers.
- Breathing or waking remains difficult after movements cease.
- A significant injury occurs or the seizure happens in water.
- The person is pregnant or has diabetes and loses consciousness.
- It is their **first known seizure**.

Call for emergency help as well when the event is followed by persistent one-sided weakness, new speech or vision difficulty, or any concern for stroke. If a person has a known seizure disorder, a familiar brief seizure may not always require an ambulance; follow their clinician-provided seizure action plan. When in doubt, prioritise safety and seek urgent advice.

## A Simple Family Plan
Families can prepare by learning seizure first aid, keeping an updated medicine list, asking whether a rescue medicine has been prescribed, and recording the person’s usual seizure pattern. Do not give rescue medicine unless it has been prescribed and the caregiver has been taught exactly how and when to use it.

For possible stroke, remember **BEFAST and 112**. For an active seizure, remember **stay, safe, side, and time**: stay with the person, make the area safe, place them on their side when appropriate, and time the event. These two responses work together without confusing one emergency with the other.

If you have experienced a first seizure, recurrent episodes, unexplained blackouts, or symptoms that may represent stroke, arrange prompt evaluation with Dr. Pratik Kishore at Neuropoint Medical Centre, New Delhi.

### References
1. CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Stroke
2. CDC: First Aid for Seizures
3. Government of India: Emergency Response Support System 112

title: Daily Strategies to Control Epilepsy and Seizures
excerpt: Epilepsy impacts 10 million Indians. From medication adherence to lifestyle routines, discover evidence-backed daily strategies — co-developed with neurologist Dr. Pratik Kishore — to reduce seizure frequency and live safely.
content:
## Understanding Epilepsy and Common Triggers
Epilepsy impacts over 10 million people in India. Seizures occur due to sudden, abnormal bursts of electrical activity in brain cells. Presentations range from generalised tonic-clonic seizures (full-body stiffening and rhythmic jerking lasting 2-3 minutes) to focal seizures (one-sided twitching, sensory tingling, or brief lapses in awareness).

Common triggers include sleep deprivation from irregular shifts, missed medication doses, high psychological stress, alcohol or tobacco use, and low blood sugar levels during prolonged fasting.

## Daily Strategies for Safe Epilepsy Management
- **Strict Medication Adherence:** Take anti-seizure medications (AEDs) exactly at the prescribed hours. Use automated reminders or pill organizers.
- **Maintain a Seizure Log:** Track the date, time, duration, preceding triggers, and post-seizure recovery in a dedicated notebook or app.
- **Consistent Sleep Hygiene:** Aim for 7-8 hours of uninterrupted sleep every night to stabilize brain electrical activity.
- **Stress Reduction:** Gentle pranayama and relaxation techniques help lower stress hormones that lower seizure thresholds.
- **Home & Road Safety:** Avoid swimming or taking baths unsupervised; avoid riding two-wheelers without clearance from your neurologist.

Consult Dr. Pratik Kishore at Neuropoint Medical Centre for advanced video-EEG monitoring and personalized seizure management.
author: Dr. Pratik Kishore

title: Conquering Chronic Migraines with Remedies and Modern Care
excerpt: Migraines affect 15% of Indian women, triggered by hormonal cycles, summer dehydration, and everyday irritants. Dr. Pratik Kishore shares a complete guide from home remedies to cutting-edge CGRP blockers.
content:
## What Causes Migraines?
Migraines cause intense, pulsating headache pain—often concentrated on one side of the head—accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light (photophobia) or sound. Attacks can last anywhere from 4 to 72 hours. In up to 25% of patients, migraines are preceded by visual auras such as flashing zig-zag lights or temporary blind spots.

Common triggers include dehydration during hot summers, skipping meals, hormonal fluctuations, strong fragrances, lack of sleep, and stress.

## Multi-Tiered Approach to Migraine Relief
- **Acute Treatments:** Triptans or targeted pain relievers taken at the earliest onset of headache give the highest success rates.
- **Preventive Therapies:** For patients suffering more than 4-6 headache days a month, preventive medications like beta-blockers, topiramate, or novel CGRP receptor antagonists significantly reduce frequency.
- **Lifestyle Adjustments:** Drink 2.5–3 liters of water daily, maintain regular meal intervals, and stick to a consistent sleep schedule.
- **Advanced Interventions:** Chronic migraine patients resistant to standard medications can benefit from peripheral nerve blocks or quarterly Botox injections.

Visit Neuropoint Medical Centre for comprehensive headache and migraine diagnosis.
author: Dr. Pratik Kishore

title: Thriving with Parkinson's: Exercise, Meds, and Family Support
excerpt: 1-2% of Indians over 60 live with Parkinson's, often misdiagnosed as age-related shakiness. Dr. Pratik Kishore explains the gold-standard treatments, DBS surgery, and practical lifestyle strategies for patients and their families.
content:
## Recognizing Parkinson's Disease Early
Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative condition resulting from progressive loss of dopamine-producing cells in the brain. Key motor symptoms include resting tremor (often described as 'pill-rolling'), muscle stiffness or rigidity, slowness of movement (bradykinesia), and balance instability.

Non-motor signs such as chronic constipation, REM sleep behavior disorders, loss of smell, and mild depression frequently emerge years before motor symptoms are identified.

## Comprehensive Treatment Strategies
- **Dopaminergic Medications:** Levodopa/Carbidopa remains the gold standard, helping replenish dopamine levels to restore fluid body movements.
- **Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS):** For advanced Parkinson's with medication fluctuations or severe tremor, DBS surgery offers life-changing motor control and reduces pill burden.
- **Targeted Physical & Speech Therapy:** Regular aerobic exercise, balance training, and LSVT BIG/LOUD therapy help maintain posture and vocal projection.
- **Family and Caregiver Support:** Establishing structured daily routines and safety-proofing the living space ensures lasting independence and safety.
author: Dr. Pratik Kishore

title: Empowering MS Patients: Symptoms, Nutrition, and Long-Term Management
excerpt: Multiple sclerosis is underdiagnosed in India, linked to low vitamin D and B12 deficiencies. Dr. Pratik Kishore walks through MRI-confirmed diagnosis, DMT therapy, and daily nutrition and exercise strategies for lasting quality of life.
content:
## What Is Multiple Sclerosis?
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disorder where the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective myelin sheath covering nerve fibers in the central nervous system. This disruption causes symptoms such as optic neuritis (blurred or painful vision), numbness, tingling sensations, chronic fatigue, muscle stiffness, and balance difficulties.

## Modern Management and Long-Term Care
- **Disease-Modifying Therapies (DMTs):** Advanced biologic infusions and oral DMTs halt relapses and protect brain and spinal tissue from long-term progression.
- **Symptom-Targeted Therapy:** Medications for spasticity, fatigue management, and neuro-physiotherapy are tailored to each patient's needs.
- **Nutrition and Vitamin D:** Correcting vitamin D and B12 deficiencies, combined with an anti-inflammatory diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids, supports optimal nerve function.
- **Heat Management:** Preventing overheating with cooling accessories and moderate exercising in climate-controlled environments prevents temporary symptom flare-ups (Uhthoff’s phenomenon).
author: Dr. Pratik Kishore
